definitions.explanation: A pair of lion-like stone statues traditionally placed at the entrance of Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples in Japan, believed to ward off evil spirits.

examples.japanese: {神社|じんじゃ}の{入|い}り{口|ぐち}に{狛犬|こまいぬ}がある。
examples.english: There are guardian lion-dogs at the entrance of the shrine.

examples.japanese: この{狛犬|こまいぬ}は{江戸|えど}{時代|じだい}に{作|つく}られた。
examples.english: This komainu was made during the Edo period.

examples.japanese: {狛犬|こまいぬ}の{一方|いっぽう}は{口|くち}を{開|あ}け、{一方|いっぽう}は{閉|と}じている。
examples.english: One komainu has its mouth open, and the other has its mouth closed.

notes:
CULTURAL NOTE:
The two {狛犬|こまいぬ} at shrine entrances represent 'a' ({阿|あ}) and 'un' ({吽|うん}):
- {阿|あ} - mouth open, beginning sound of Sanskrit alphabet
- {吽|うん} - mouth closed, ending sound
Together they represent the beginning and end of all things, similar to 'alpha and omega.'

ORIGIN: The name {狛犬|こまいぬ} comes from {高麗|こま} (Goryeo/Korea), reflecting the continental Asian origin of these guardian figures.

RELATED SHRINE/TEMPLE ELEMENTS:
- {鳥居|とりい} (torii gate)
- {灯籠|とうろう} (stone lantern)
- {手水舎|ちょうずや} (purification fountain)
- {参道|さんどう} (approach path to shrine)

SIMILAR GUARDIAN FIGURES:
- シーサー (Okinawan lion-dog)
- {獅子|しし} (lion statue - often at temples)
